Consult Summary:
- 32-year-old man with ~1.5–2 months of recurrent, transient right upper-limb paresthesia/numbness and episodic unilateral weakness with concurrent intermittent gait disturbance and recent difficulty holding/using a cup — referred urgently for suspected transient ischemic attack (TIA).

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Recurrent episodes of pins-and-needles and numbness in the right hand with subjective right arm weakness.
  - Concurrent episodes of right-sided leg weakness/abnormal gait noted by a colleague during the same episodes.
  - Increasing frequency of episodes over past 1.5–2 months.
- Timeline / progression:
  - Symptoms began approximately 1.5–2 months ago.
  - Initially occasional (approx. once a month to once a week); frequency has increased to several episodes per day.
  - Individual episodes last a few days (patient reports weakness lasts a few days then returns to normal).
  - Fatigue reported early in course (brief periods of tiredness lasting a couple of days).
  - Over the past couple of days, patient reports difficulty holding his cup and mildly harder drinking during episodes (only during episodes).
  - At time of consultation patient was asymptomatic.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - None specifically identified in the consultation.
- Associated symptoms:
  - Nausea and reduced motivation reported intermittently.
  - Sensation of “something in my throat” during episodes.
  - No current or reported difficulty speaking.
  - No clear visual disturbance reported (patient wears glasses; did not report acute visual changes).
- Systems review / pertinent negatives:
  - No reported difficulty swallowing aside from throat sensation.
  - No reported speech impairment during episodes.
  - No reported persistent visual loss.
  - No other systemic complaints documented.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic medical diagnoses reported.
- Previous screening after father's carotid surgery: blood tests for cholesterol, diabetes, and blood pressure check were performed and reported as normal by the patient (no numeric values documented).
- No prior personal history of stroke or TIA reported.

Medications:
- Aspirin 75 mg once daily — patient self-initiated (dose and frequency stated by patient).
- No other medications reported.
- Medication reconciliation incomplete (no pharmacy list or other prescriptions documented).

Allergies:
- Allergic to penicillin only.

Social History:
- Occupation: medical doctor, specialty: plastic surgery.
- Lives with wife; not living alone.
- Smoking: denies tobacco use.
- Alcohol/substance use: not documented.
- Patient contacted clinician after internet searching; started aspirin independently after father’s carotid procedure.

Family History:
- Father underwent carotid surgery (“operation to the side of his neck to reduce the risk of stroke”).

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: not documented.
- Examination findings: none documented (no neurological examination or other physical exam recorded in the transcript).

Investigations:
- No investigations performed during this consultation.
- Planned/anticipated investigations discussed as part of TIA clinic evaluation:
  - Carotid artery ultrasound (Doppler).
  - Possible brain imaging (to exclude intracranial hemorrhage or other pathology).
  - Additional tests as arranged by TIA clinic.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Suspected transient ischemic attacks (TIA) / mini-stroke
  - Assessment:
    - Clinical picture consistent with recurrent transient focal neurological episodes: right hand paresthesia/numbness, transient right arm and leg weakness, abnormal gait, with increasing frequency and recent functional impact (difficulty holding cup) — concern for TIA.
  - Plan:
    - Urgent referral to TIA clinic made during the consultation.
    - Expectation communicated that the TIA clinic will contact the patient within 1–2 days (attempt to be seen within the next 1–2 days; practical turnaround targeted before the weekend).
    - TIA clinic evaluation to include carotid ultrasound and possibly brain imaging; further tests as per clinic protocol.
    - Patient advised to attend Emergency Department immediately if symptoms recur and are prolonged/persistent (concern for possible stroke rather than transient event).
    - Patient advised they may contact the hospital (PALS/TIA clinic number to be placed in the consultation notes) to check appointment scheduling and to chase the referral.
    - Patient advised they may contact the GP service for telephone advice or reassessment if new/worsening symptoms or if there is delay in being contacted.
- Issue 2: Patient self-initiated aspirin use
  - Assessment:
    - Patient has been taking aspirin 75 mg daily on his own initiative after his father's carotid procedure; he has not previously discussed this with his GP.
  - Plan:
    - Aspirin 75 mg daily recorded in consultation notes.
    - Patient instructed to ensure clinicians at the TIA clinic / receiving service are aware of current aspirin use when contacted/seen.
- Issue 3: (Administrative / access)
  - Assessment:
    - Need for prompt outpatient assessment and clear communication channels to avoid delay.
  - Plan:
    - Doctor to send referral to TIA clinic during this consultation.
    - Clinic contact details (PALS / TIA clinic number) to be left in the consultation notes for patient use.
    - Patient advised to phone the clinic/hospital today or tomorrow morning to confirm scheduling if desired.
    - Offer of telephone follow-up or prompt re-contact with GP practice if patient not contacted or if symptoms recur.

Quality checks / document_quality:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, oxygen saturation) were not recorded.
  - Formal neurological examination and findings (cranial nerves, motor strength, tone, reflexes, coordination, gait assessment) not documented.
  - Exact dates for onset of first episode and timing of progression not precisely documented (patient estimates 1.5–2 months).
  - No imaging or laboratory results available.
  - Comprehensive medication list and doses beyond aspirin not documented.
  - No documentation of anticoagulation/antiplatelet management plan beyond referral.
- Internal conflicts from the transcript:
  - Minor inconsistency/unclear phrasing regarding prior episode frequency ("maybe once a week, to once a month") — frequency reported to have increased to multiple episodes per day more recently.
- Transcript quality comment:
  - Intermittent audio/video connection issues noted during the consultation; overall content intelligible but brief dropouts and repetitions occurred.
